claim: Wild-type 1.5-fold stage embryos display a shallow pit (sensory depression) approximately 2.1 µm deep in the region corresponding to the location of the future mouth.
source: In wild-type embryos at the 1.5-fold stage of development, a shallow pit (∼2.1 µm deep), termed the sensory depression, is detected in the region corresponding to the location of the future mouth (buccal cavity; Figure 1A, Table 1; Sulston et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements presented in Table 1 showing ingression depth of 2.12 ± 0.23 μm for wild-type 1.5-fold embryos, and is also cited from Sulston et al., 1983.

claim: The sensory depression is relatively short-lived and is no longer visible in threefold-stage embryos.
source: This morphological feature is relatively short-lived and is no longer visible in threefold-stage embryos (Figure 1A, Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A and Figure 2C, and by data in Table 1 showing ingression depth of 0.26 ± 0.096 μm for wild-type 3.0-fold embryos.

claim: mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 embryos have a striking keyhole-shaped invagination approximately 4.3 µm deep at the 1.5-fold stage.
source: In contrast, mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 embryos had a striking keyhole-shaped invagination in this region, which increased in depth between the 1.5-fold (∼4.3 µm) and 3-fold (∼9.5 µm) stages (Figure 1A, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements in Table 1 showing ingression depths of 4.25 ± 0.89 μm for mec-8; sym-3 and 4.27 ± 1.16 μm for mec-8; sym-4 at 1.5-fold stage, and by images in Figure 1A.

claim: The keyhole-shaped invagination in mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 embryos increases in depth to approximately 9.5 µm at the 3-fold stage.
source: In contrast, mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 embryos had a striking keyhole-shaped invagination in this region, which increased in depth between the 1.5-fold (∼4.3 µm) and 3-fold (∼9.5 µm) stages (Figure 1A, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements in Table 1 showing ingression depths of 9.82 ± 0.68 μm for mec-8; sym-3 and 9.19 ± 0.83 μm for mec-8; sym-4 at 3.0-fold stage.

claim: mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 L1 larvae display the 'Pharynx ingressed' (Pin) phenotype, in which the pharynx and buccal capsule are displaced toward the posterior end of the animal.
source: In contrast to wild-type L1 larvae, in which the pharynx and associated buccal capsule (terminal mouth part) extended to the anterior tip of the worm, mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 L1 larvae displayed what we have termed the 'Pharynx ingressed' (Pin) phenotype, in which the pharynx and buccal capsule are displaced toward the posterior end of the animal (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A showing the Pin phenotype in mec-8; sym-3 L1 larvae.

claim: In Pin larvae, lateral anterior tissues fold over and surround the ingressed buccal capsule, preventing double mutants from feeding.
source: In Pin larvae, lateral anterior tissues appeared to fold over and surround the ingressed buccal capsule, thereby preventing double mutants from feeding (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observations in Figure 1A and the description of the morphological defect.

claim: The Pin defects were observed at only low frequencies in sym-3, sym-4 and mec-8 single mutants.
source: Although these defects were observed at only low frequencies in sym-3, sym-4 and mec-8 single mutants, they were highly penetrant in mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 double mutants (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1B showing low percentages of Pin in single mutants (sym-3: ~5%, sym-4: ~7%, mec-8: ~15%) compared to double mutants.

claim: The Pin defects were highly penetrant in mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 double mutants.
source: Although these defects were observed at only low frequencies in sym-3, sym-4 and mec-8 single mutants, they were highly penetrant in mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 double mutants (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1B showing high percentages of Pin in double mutants (mec-8; sym-3: ~98%, mec-8; sym-4: ~95%).

claim: The pharynx lengthens along its anteroposterior axis during embryonic development, transforming from a blunt conical shape into a bi-lobed structure.
source: During embryonic development, the pharynx lengthens along its anteroposterior axis, transforming from a blunt conical shape into a bi-lobed structure that is attached to the mouth at the anterior and to the intestine in the mid body (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the schematic representation in Figure 1C showing pharyngeal morphology changes during development.

claim: The pharynx is attached to the mouth at the anterior and to the intestine in the mid body.
source: During embryonic development, the pharynx lengthens along its anteroposterior axis, transforming from a blunt conical shape into a bi-lobed structure that is attached to the mouth at the anterior and to the intestine in the mid body (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description and schematic in Figure 1C.

claim: Lengthening of the pharynx is facilitated in part by an outward-directed pulling force exerted by the anterior epidermis as the embryo undergoes elongation.
source: We hypothesized that lengthening of the pharynx is facilitated in part by an outward-directed pulling force that is exerted by the anterior epidermis as the embryo undergoes elongation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their model, supported by subsequent experimental evidence.

claim: As the pharynx is stretched, it exerts a counter inward-pulling force on the embryonic epidermis.
source: In addition, as the pharynx is stretched, it exerts a counter inward-pulling force on the embryonic epidermis.
evidence: This is part of the authors' model, which is subsequently tested and supported by experimental evidence including FRET measurements and genetic manipulations.

claim: The inward-pulling force exerted by the pharynx is greatest in the region where the pharynx attaches to the epidermis, contributing to the formation of the sensory depression.
source: This inward-pulling force would be greatest in the region where the pharynx attaches to the epidermis, contributing to the formation of the sensory depression (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is part of the authors' model, supported by FRET measurements showing higher tension at the sensory depression region.

claim: Prevention of pharyngeal-epidermal attachment suppresses keyhole formation in mec-8; sym-3 embryos.
source: As predicted, formation of the keyhole was suppressed in mec-8; pha-1(tm3671); sym-3 triple mutants in which the pharynx failed to attach (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A and Table 1 showing that 85% of mec-8; pha-1(tm3671); sym-3 embryos that failed to form pharyngeal-epidermal attachment did not develop keyholes.

claim: In mec-8; pha-1(tm3671); sym-3 embryos in which the pharynx was attached to the epidermis (∼15%), a keyhole was observed.
source: In contrast, in mec-8; pha-1(tm3671); sym-3 embryos in which the pharynx was attached to the epidermis (∼15%), a keyhole was observed, indicating that the loss of attachment per se, rather than the loss of pha-1 activity, was responsible for the suppression of keyhole formation in the majority of triple mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing that the 15% of embryos that formed pharyngeal-epidermal attachment developed keyholes.

claim: Early-stage mec-8; pha-1(e2123); sym-3 triple mutants formed a stereotypical keyhole.
source: As predicted by our model, early-stage mec-8; pha-1(e2123); sym-3 triple mutants formed a stereotypical keyhole, consistent with the presence of a pharyngeal-epidermal connection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and data in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: The absence of a keyhole or Pin phenotype in late-stage mec-8; pha-1(e2123); sym-3 embryos and L1 larvae indicates that anterior ingression of the epidermis requires a sustained pulling force exerted by the pharynx.
source: The absence of a keyhole or Pin phenotype in late-stage embryos and L1 larvae, however, indicated that anterior ingression of the epidermis requires a sustained pulling force exerted by the pharynx and that the keyholes are not static once formed (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and Table 1 showing that mec-8; pha-1(e2123); sym-3 embryos lose the keyhole after pharyngeal detachment.

claim: The depth of the keyhole in mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 mutants steadily increased from the comma stage to the threefold stage of embryogenesis.
source: We also observed that the depth of the keyhole in mec-8; sym-3 and mec-8; sym-4 mutants steadily increased from the comma stage to the threefold stage of embryogenesis (Figure 1A, Figure 2C, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data in Figure 2C and measurements in Table 1.

claim: Inhibition of embryonic elongation past the twofold stage by let-502(RNAi) prevents further deepening of the keyhole in mec-8; sym-4 mutants.
source: After morphogenetic arrest, however, keyholes in mec-8; sym-4; let-502(RNAi) embryos failed to deepen, indicating that the progressive increase in keyhole depth is a function of embryonic elongation, rather than the passage of time.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing that keyhole depth plateaus after let-502(RNAi) treatment arrests elongation.

claim: Reversal of embryonic elongation in mec-8; sqt-3(e2117ts) mutants leads to a decrease in keyhole depth.
source: Consistent with our model, keyholes reached a maximum depth of ∼8–10 µm at around the threefold stage but then shrunk to ∼4–6 µm after a partial reversal of embryonic elongation (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2D showing keyhole depth decreases as embryos undergo reversal of elongation.

claim: Wild-type 1.5-fold embryos had significantly higher tension (lower FRET) at the sensory depression region (SDR) as compared with regions outside the sensory depression (p = 0.0008).
source: In contrast, wild-type 1.5-fold embryos had significantly higher tension (lower FRET) at the SDR as compared with regions outside the sensory depression (p = 0.0008), consistent with the hypothesis that pharyngeal attachment contributes to the force balance at the sensory depression (Figure 3C,D,I; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET measurements presented in Figure 3 and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 1.5-fold pha-1(0) mutants in which the pharynx failed to attach did not display appreciably lower levels of mechanical tension at the SDR as compared with regions outside the sensory depression (p = 0.2421).
source: In contrast, 1.5-fold pha-1(0) mutants in which the pharynx failed to attach did not display appreciably lower levels of mechanical tension at the SDR as compared with regions outside the sensory depression (p = 0.2421; Figure 3G,H,I; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET measurements presented in Figure 3 and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Tension at the SDR was significantly higher in wild-type embryos as compared with the SDR region in pha-1(0) mutants at the 1.5-fold stage (p < 0.0001).
source: In addition, tension at the SDR was significantly higher in wild-type embryos as compared with the SDR region in pha-1(0) mutants at the 1.5-fold (p < 0.0001) but not early comma stages (p = 1.000; Supplementary file 2), also consistent with pharyngeal attachment and pulling leading to tension at the anterior epidermis.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET measurements and statistical analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: No significant differences in UNC-70(TSMod) FRET efficiency were observed between the sensory depression region (SDR) and non-SDR region prior to the attachment of the pharynx to the epidermis (early comma stage) in either wild-type or pha-1(0) embryos.
source: No significant differences in UNC-70(TSMod) FRET efficiency were observed between the sensory depression region (SDR) and non-SDR region prior to the attachment of the pharynx to the epidermis (early comma stage) in either wild-type or pha-1(0) embryos (Figure 3E,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET measurements presented in Figure 3E and 3I.

claim: The tiling array identified 1106 individual regions within a total of 449 genes that were differentially expressed (>1.5-fold) between wild-type and mec-8 embryos.
source: We identified 1106 individual regions within a total of 449 genes that were differentially expressed (>1.5-fold) between wild-type and mec-8 embryos (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by tiling array data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Among the 449 identified genes, 135 (30%) are annotated by WormBase as having multiple (alternatively spliced) isoforms.
source: Among the 449 identified genes, 135 (30%) are annotated by WormBase as having multiple (alternatively spliced) isoforms (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of tiling array data and WormBase annotations presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: MEC-8 is required for normal splicing events within the region encompassing exons 14 through 19 of fbn-1.
source: Thus MEC-8 is required for normal splicing events within the region encompassing exons 14 through 19 of fbn-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR analysis in Figure 4B showing aberrant splicing patterns in mec-8 mutants.

claim: Splicing between exons 16 and 17 was largely abolished in mec-8 mutants.
source: Consistent with a reduction in splicing efficiency, splicing between exons 16 and 17 was largely abolished in mec-8 mutants (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR analysis in Figure 4B showing absence of expected bands in mec-8 mutants.

claim: Splicing between exons 19 and 20 was unaffected in mec-8 mutants.
source: In contrast, splicing between exons 19 and 20 was unaffected in mec-8 mutants, consistent with both the tiling array findings and the absence of known alternative splicing events between these exons (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR analysis in Figure 4B showing normal splicing patterns between exons 19 and 20 in mec-8 mutants.

claim: Expression of an fbn-1 cDNA (e isoform) driven by native fbn-1 promoter sequences partially rescued the synthetic lethality of mec-8; sym-4 mutants in two independent lines.
source: Most notably, expression of an fbn-1 cDNA (e isoform) driven by native fbn-1 promoter sequences partially rescued the synthetic lethality of mec-8; sym-4 mutants in two independent lines (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data in Figure 1B showing reduced Pin phenotype in mec-8; sym-4 mutants carrying fbn-1 rescue constructs.

claim: FBN-1 is composed of many calcium-binding and non-calcium-binding EGF-like repeats.
source: FBN-1 is composed of many calcium-binding and non-calcium-binding EGF-like repeats, which are found in many matrix proteins and the extracellular domains of transmembrane proteins (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Davis, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein domain analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and cited from Davis, 1990.

claim: FBN-1 shares greatest sequence similarity with the family of latent TGFβ binding proteins (LTBPs), which include LTBP-1, -2 and -4 and fibrillins 1–3.
source: Comparison of the predicted FBN-1 peptide sequence with mammalian sequences revealed greatest sequence similarity with the family of latent TGFβ binding proteins (LTBPs), which include LTBP-1, -2 and -4 and fibrillins 1–3 (Rifkin, 2005; Todorovic et al., 2005; Hynes, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison analysis and cited from multiple references.

claim: C. elegans FBN-1 differs from other LTBP proteins by lacking the TGFβ binding domains and by having a zona pellucida (ZP) domain.
source: C. elegans FBN-1 differs from the other LTBP proteins by lacking the TGFβ binding domains and by having a zona pellucida (ZP) domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein domain analysis shown in Figure 4C and sequence comparison.

claim: ZP domains are found in many apical ECM proteins and are thought to mediate polymerization, resulting in the formation of protein fibrils.
source: ZP domains are found in many apical ECM proteins and are thought to mediate polymerization, resulting in the formation of protein fibrils (Plaza et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is cited from Plaza et al., 2010.

claim: The presence of a furin cleavage site in FBN-1 immediately after the ZP domain suggests that the extracellular domain of FBN-1 can be secreted.
source: The presence of a furin cleavage site in FBN-1 immediately after the ZP domain suggests that the extracellular domain of FBN-1 can be secreted (Figure 4C; also see below).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the presence of a furin cleavage site shown in Figure 4C and knowledge about furin protease function.

claim: Strains containing either missense allele ns67 or ns283 exhibited the Pin phenotype in ∼45% of their progeny.
source: Strikingly, strains containing either missense allele ns67 or ns283 exhibited the Pin phenotype in ∼45% of their progeny, whereas tm290 homozygotes produced by homozygous mothers carrying a rescuing fbn-1(+) extrachromosomal array had a lower percentage of Pin larvae (∼20% within the population of array-minus progeny; Figure 5B,C; Table 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5B showing Pin percentages for fbn-1 alleles.

claim: fbn-1(tm290) homozygotes produced by homozygous mothers carrying a rescuing fbn-1(+) extrachromosomal array had a lower percentage of Pin larvae (∼20% within the population of array-minus progeny).
source: Strikingly, strains containing either missense allele ns67 or ns283 exhibited the Pin phenotype in ∼45% of their progeny, whereas tm290 homozygotes produced by homozygous mothers carrying a rescuing fbn-1(+) extrachromosomal array had a lower percentage of Pin larvae (∼20% within the population of array-minus progeny; Figure 5B,C; Table 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5B.

claim: All three alleles of fbn-1 led to formation of the keyhole in embryos.
source: In addition, all three alleles of fbn-1 led to formation of the keyhole in embryos (Figure 5C, Table 1, Supplementary file 1, data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 5C, Table 1, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The percentage of Pin animals in fbn-1 double mutants with sym-3, sym-4 and mec-8 ranged from 97–100%.
source: The percentage of Pin animals in double mutants ranged from 97–100%, consistent with the enhancement observed for fbn-1(RNAi) in RNAi-hypersensitive backgrounds (Figure 5A–C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: mec-8; fbn-1(tm290) mutants arrested uniformly as embryos and failed to complete embryonic elongation.
source: Interestingly, mec-8; fbn-1(tm290) mutants arrested uniformly as embryos and failed to complete embryonic elongation (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations and images in Figure 5C.

claim: By the ∼threefold stage, 92% (n = 73) of mec-8; fbn-1(tm290) embryos exhibited prominent epidermal ingressions and furrows, which were often regularly spaced.
source: These embryos displayed a deep keyhole by the 1.5-fold stage (Table 1 and Supplementary file 1), and by the ∼threefold stage 92% (n = 73) exhibited prominent epidermal ingressions and furrows, which were often regularly spaced (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative observations and images in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibition of epidermal actomyosin contraction using let-502(RNAi) reduced the frequency of mec-8; fbn-1(tm290) embryos that contained deep furrows to 17% (n = 52).
source: Consistent with this interpretation, inhibition of epidermal actomyosin contraction using let-502(RNAi) reduced the frequency of mec-8; fbn-1(tm290) embryos that contained deep furrows to 17% (n = 52; Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of furrow phenotype by let-502(RNAi) in Figure 5C.

claim: Both systemic and epidermal-specific fbn-1(RNAi) led to an increased percentage of Pin animals in the mec-8 background.
source: Although RNAi of fbn-1 failed to produce any visible phenotype in these strains, enhancement of the Pin phenotype was observed in an NR222 derivative that carried a mec-8 mutation (p < 0.01), implicating the epidermis as critical for fbn-1 activity (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi data in Figure 6A showing enhancement of Pin in mec-8 mutants with both systemic and epidermal-specific RNAi.

claim: Based on mosaic analysis, fbn-1 activity is focused in hyp6, the anterior portion of the hyp7 syncytium, or both hyp6 and hyp7.
source: Based on numerous mosaics, fbn-1 activity is focused in hyp6, the anterior portion of the hyp7 syncytium, or both hyp6 and hyp7.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic mosaic analysis data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Pfbn-1::GFP-PEST expression was first detected in epidermal cells at the onset of embryonic morphogenesis, and expression continued throughout embryogenesis.
source: Pfbn-1::GFP-PEST expression was first detected in epidermal cells at the onset of embryonic morphogenesis, and expression continued throughout embryogenesis (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 6D showing GFP expression patterns.

claim: mini-fbn-1::mCherry localized to the apical surface of epidermal cells coincident with the location of the embryonic sheath.
source: mini-fbn-1::mCherry localized to the apical surface of epidermal cells coincident with the location of the embryonic sheath (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 6D showing mCherry localization.

claim: mini-fbn-1::mCherry expression was first detected during early stages of morphogenesis and increased in intensity through the 1.5-fold stage.
source: Expression was first detected during early stages of morphogenesis and increased in intensity through the 1.5-fold stage, consistent with the timing of embryonic sheath formation (Figure 6D; Priess and Hirsh, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 6D and cited from Priess and Hirsh, 1986.

claim: mini-fbn-1::mCherry was detected in the extra-embryonic space of early morphogenetic embryos, consistent with apical secretion of the fusion proteins.
source: Notably, mini-fbn-1::mCherry was detected in the extra-embryonic space of early morphogenetic embryos, consistent with apical secretion of the fusion proteins (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 6D showing mCherry signal outside the embryo.

claim: Keyholes were detected in ∼1.5-fold to 3.0-fold-stage embryos treated with chitinase and trypsin.
source: Most notably, we detected keyholes in ∼1.5-fold to 3.0-fold-stage embryos, as well as mild ingressions at the surface of some embryos (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and images in Figure 7A showing keyholes in trypsin-treated embryos.

claim: The penetrance of Pin was ∼10-fold higher in embryos treated with both trypsin and chitinase relative to chitinase alone.
source: Nevertheless, the penetrance of Pin was ∼10-fold higher in embryos treated with both trypsin and chitinase relative to chitinase alone (data not shown), consistent with a role for sheath proteins in preventing mechanical deformation of cells surrounding the sensory depression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing treatment conditions.

claim: UNC-70, a β-spectrin ortholog, is expressed widely during embryogenesis and acts together with α-spectrin and actin to form a subcortical cytoskeletal network.
source: UNC-70, a β-spectrin ortholog, is expressed widely during embryogenesis and acts together with α-spectrin and actin to form a subcortical cytoskeletal network that is critical for cell shape and mechanics in a variety of cell types in C. elegans (Bretscher, 1991; Hammarlund et al., 2000; Moorthy et al., 2000; Norman and Moerman, 2002).
evidence: The claim is cited from multiple references describing UNC-70 function.

claim: The UNC-70(TSMod) fusion protein localized to the cell membrane cortex in a pattern that was seemingly identical to immunostaining of endogenous UNC-70.
source: Importantly, the UNC-70(TSMod) fusion protein localized to the cell membrane cortex in a pattern that was seemingly identical to immunostaining of endogenous UNC-70 (Moorthy et al., 2000), with a prominent accumulation at future location of the buccal cavity (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published immunostaining data and images in Figure 3B.

claim: UNC-70(TSMod) rescued the severely paralyzed locomotion phenotype of unc-70 null mutant animals.
source: Moreover, UNC-70(TSMod) rescued the severely paralyzed locomotion phenotype of unc-70 null mutant animals, indicating that the fusion protein is functional (Krieg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional rescue data cited from Krieg et al., 2014.

claim: The embryonic sheath is required to prevent excessive constriction and deformation of the epidermis by actomyosin ring contraction.
source: Notably, the apical ECM (aECM) of the embryonic epidermis, termed the embryonic sheath, is required to prevent excessive constriction and deformation of the epidermis by actomyosin ring contraction (Priess and Hirsh, 1986).
evidence: The claim is cited from Priess and Hirsh, 1986.

claim: Ring-shaped actomyosin bundles, which are spaced regularly along the anteroposterior axis of the embryo, undergo coordinated contraction leading to circumferential constriction of the embryo.
source: Shortly after this stage, ring-shaped actomyosin bundles, which are spaced regularly along the anteroposterior axis of the embryo, undergo coordinated contraction. This contraction leads to the circumferential constriction of the embryo and its conversion to a tapered cylindrical (fusiform) shape that is ∼250 µm long (about five times the length of the egg shell; Costa et al., 1997; Priess and Hirsh, 1986).
evidence: The claim is cited from Costa et al., 1997 and Priess and Hirsh, 1986.

claim: Linkage of the pharynx to the mouth and epidermis is established between the comma and 1.5-fold stages (∼380–410 min).
source: Linkage of the pharynx to the mouth and epidermis is established between the comma and 1.5-fold stages (∼380–410 min; Figure 1C, data not shown; Sulston et al., 1983; Portereiko and Mango, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental timing data and cited from Sulston et al., 1983 and Portereiko and Mango, 2001.

claim: Mutations in human fibrillin genes lead to connective tissue disorders including Marfan syndrome.
source: Notably, mutations in human fibrillin genes lead to connective tissue disorders including Marfan syndrome (Dietz et al., 2005; Ramirez and Dietz, 2009; Ramirez and Sakai, 2010).
evidence: The claim is cited from multiple references on Marfan syndrome.

claim: sym-3 and sym-4 encode conserved proteins with predicted roles in vesicular trafficking.
source: Whereas sym-3 and sym-4 encode conserved proteins with predicted roles in vesicular trafficking (Yochem et al., 2004; also see 'Discussion'), mec-8 encodes a conserved RNA-binding protein involved in alternative splicing (Lundquist et al., 1996; Spike et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is cited from Yochem et al., 2004 and discussed in the manuscript.

claim: mec-8 encodes a conserved RNA-binding protein involved in alternative splicing.
source: Whereas sym-3 and sym-4 encode conserved proteins with predicted roles in vesicular trafficking (Yochem et al., 2004; also see 'Discussion'), mec-8 encodes a conserved RNA-binding protein involved in alternative splicing (Lundquist et al., 1996; Spike et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is cited from Lundquist et al., 1996 and Spike et al., 2002.

claim: FBN-1 is a ZP domain protein related to vertebrate fibrillins.
source: Resistance of the epidermis to this force and to actomyosin-based circumferential constricting forces is mediated by FBN-1, a ZP domain protein related to vertebrate fibrillins.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein domain analysis and sequence comparison presented in the manuscript.

claim: fbn-1 was required specifically within the epidermis.
source: fbn-1 was required specifically within the epidermis and FBN-1 was expressed in epidermal cells and secreted to the apical surface as a putative component of the embryonic sheath.
evidence: The claim is supported by epidermal-specific RNAi data in Figure 6A and mosaic analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: FBN-1 was expressed in epidermal cells and secreted to the apical surface as a putative component of the embryonic sheath.
source: fbn-1 was required specifically within the epidermis and FBN-1 was expressed in epidermal cells and secreted to the apical surface as a putative component of the embryonic sheath.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data in Figure 6D showing Pfbn-1::GFP-PEST in epidermal cells and mini-fbn-1::mCherry at the apical surface.

claim: Tiling array studies indicated that fbn-1 mRNA processing requires the conserved alternative splicing factor MEC-8/RBPMS.
source: Tiling array studies indicated that fbn-1 mRNA processing requires the conserved alternative splicing factor MEC-8/RBPMS.
evidence: The claim is supported by tiling array data and PCR analysis in Figure 4 showing aberrant fbn-1 splicing in mec-8 mutants.

claim: The conserved SYM-3/FAM102A and SYM-4/WDR44 proteins, which are linked to protein trafficking, function as additional components of this network.
source: The conserved SYM-3/FAM102A and SYM-4/WDR44 proteins, which are linked to protein trafficking, function as additional components of this network.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data showing synthetic phenotypes in double mutants and discussion of protein function.

claim: The apical extracellular matrix is important in preventing mechanical deformation of the epidermis during development.
source: Our studies demonstrate the importance of the apical extracellular matrix in preventing mechanical deformation of the epidermis during development.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by all the experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.
